label: Voronoi Diagrams: Proximity, Duality, Lifting
notes: Open by naming the three views students should keep synchronized. The Voronoi diagram answers nearest-site questions in the plane, the Delaunay triangulation records which cells touch, and lifting to the paraboloid explains why empty circles and convex hulls are part of the same story.

label: Applications Preview
notes: Use this slide to justify the chapter before definitions take over. Nearest neighbors, spanning trees, and largest empty circles look like different tasks, but the Voronoi-Delaunay structure makes them share candidate edges and candidate centers. The point is not that one diagram solves everything automatically; it gives the right sparse geometry to search.

label: Definition Slide
notes: Start from the inequality, then translate every symbol into geometry. A point belongs to the cell of p_i if no other site is closer. Equality with one other site makes an edge; equality with two other sites makes a vertex in the usual nondegenerate setting.

label: Half-Plane Construction
notes: Derive the half-plane only far enough to show why the boundary is linear. Squaring the distance comparison cancels the x dot x term, leaving a linear inequality. This single cancellation explains convex cells, polygonal boundaries, and the baseline half-plane-intersection algorithm.

label: Bounded And Unbounded Cells
notes: Connect this to the previous convex hull chapters. A hull site has a supporting line, so moving outward normal to that line keeps the site nearest forever and the cell is unbounded. Interior sites have competitors in every direction, so their regions can close up.

label: Degeneracy And Delaunay Flip
notes: Use this as the chapter's robustness checkpoint. In general position, three sites define a Voronoi vertex and a Delaunay triangle. With four cocircular sites, the empty-circle test is tied, and either diagonal can be selected. The flip is the visible symptom of crossing that degeneracy.

label: Delaunay As Dual
notes: Make the dual construction concrete. We are not drawing abstract graph dual edges through every face; we connect the two sites whose cells share a Voronoi edge. In the nondegenerate case those connections are straight, planar, and form the Delaunay triangulation.

label: Linear Size Roadmap
notes: Give students the counting strategy rather than a wall of formulas. Once the Delaunay dual is planar, Euler-style accounting controls the number of edges and triangular faces. The Voronoi diagram inherits that linear bound because its ridges and vertices correspond to dual features.

label: Empty-Circle Theorem
notes: Treat empty circles as certificates students can inspect. The center is a Voronoi vertex because it is equidistant from the triangle sites; emptiness says no other site is closer. That is exactly the local condition needed for the triangle to belong to the Delaunay triangulation.

label: Algorithm Families
notes: Position the algorithms as families of invariants. Half-plane intersection follows the definition directly. Divide-and-conquer and Fortune's sweep achieve optimal planar bounds with different data structures. Lifting and arrangements are less about a simple coding recipe here and more about revealing why Voronoi geometry belongs with convex hulls and envelopes.

label: Fortune Sweep Intuition
notes: Avoid drowning the class in implementation details on the first pass. The key intuition is that a point on the beach line is equally far from a site and from the sweep line, so the arcs are parabolas. Breakpoints between arcs trace Voronoi edges; site and circle events are the moments when the combinatorial beach line changes.

label: Nearest Neighbors And MST
notes: Explain this as a reduction in search space. The complete Euclidean graph has every pair of sites, but the Delaunay graph keeps only geometrically plausible neighbors. If an MST edge or nearest-neighbor edge were not Delaunay, an empty-circle or cut argument would reveal a closer replacement.

label: Largest Empty Circle
notes: Treat the largest empty circle as an optimization problem over the distance-to-nearest-site function. Away from Voronoi features, the center can usually move to increase the radius. At a Voronoi vertex, several sites constrain the radius at once, making it a natural candidate for a local maximum.

label: Medial Axis
notes: Use the medial axis to broaden the meaning of site. Instead of nearest point among a finite set, the distance is to polygon boundary features. The same equal-distance idea identifies centers of maximal circles, and those centers form a skeletal representation of the shape.

label: Paraboloid Lifting
notes: Connect the chapter to the hull chapters explicitly. The paraboloid turns circle emptiness in the plane into a supporting-plane condition in three dimensions. Lower hull facets are exactly the lifted triples whose projected circumcircles are empty.

label: Tangent Planes And Arrangements
notes: Show the algebraic continuity across the lecture. The distance comparison, the tangent plane, and the envelope view all come from the same squared-distance cancellation. This prepares students for arrangements: instead of one diagram in the plane, we study cells made by many curves, lines, or planes.

label: Applied Lab And Recap
notes: Close by asking students to move between the views without changing the object. A cell is a nearest-site region, an edge in the dual is an empty-circle certificate, and a lifted lower facet is the same relationship seen from three dimensions. The lab prompts turn those equivalences into experiments students can rerun.
